extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, journalists, and policymakers interested in public opinion and democratic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about how public opinion is formed, validated, and limited in democratic societies; the text addresses conditions under which democratic self-government can be informed and reliable. Useful for scholars, analysts, and designers of public-information institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate private versions before acting
rubrics_metrics.description: The central problem is not merely to 'transmit the force of individual opinion into public action' but the more momentous question 'how to validate our private versions' of the political scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before converting private opinion into public action, individuals and institutions must test and validate those private versions; this requires conscious methods of checking and corroboration rather than immediate acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exact record, measurement, analysis and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound method of political thought should be 'based on exact record, measurement, analysis and comparison.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realistic public opinion depends on quantitative and comparative evidence rather than on intuition or tradition; employ records, measurement, and comparative analysis when forming or evaluating opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop self-criticism and analyze opinions in formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction in the need for better ideas 'grows as self-criticism increases' and 'makes us conscious of buncombe... and on guard to detect it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should 'learn to use knowledge of the way opinions are put together to watch over our own opinions when they are being put together' — practice analyzing one's own opinions when reading, talking, and deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust casual opinion born of partial contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Casual opinion is described as 'the product of partial contact, of tradition, and personal interests' and thus does not readily accept methods based on record and measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that opinions formed from limited local experience, tradition, or self-interest are unreliable for complex or distant public matters and require supplementation by better information and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic judgment limited to direct and certain knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The author asserts that 'the only environment in which spontaneous politics were possible was one confined within the range of the ruler's direct and certain knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spontaneous, uninstructed democratic judgment can only be expected to work where issues lie within the direct experience and certain knowledge of the citizens; beyond that range formal information and intermediaries are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: For spontaneous democracy, environment must be simple and self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'democracy is to be spontaneous, the interests of democracy must . . . approximate those of the township' and the environment 'must be confined within the range of every man's direct and certain knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where democratic self-government is to function without extensive mediation, public affairs should be intelligible, local, and manageable by ordinary citizens; complex, far‑flung issues need mediated reporting and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments of knowledge are essential (recording, measurement, canons of evidence, psychological analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes the importance of 'measurement and . . . record, quantitative and comparative analysis, the canons of evidence, and the ability of psychological analysis to correct and discount the prejudices of the witness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To extend reliable public judgment beyond small communities, societies must develop institutions and techniques—continuous reporting, measurement, evidence rules, and psychological insight—to bring unseen affairs into judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limited attention and partial experience of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Political theory had to assume 'no man could have more than a very partial experience of public affairs' and that people 'can give only a little time to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design civic processes and information flows with the recognition that individuals have limited time and attention; prioritize clear, salient information and institutional supports for complex decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of the 'omnicompetent citizen' stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic doctrine historically assumed 'one man was as competent as the next' (the 'omnicompetent citizen'), an assumption that works in simple rural townships but fails when universally applied to complex societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming universal competence; allow for division of labor, expertise, and institutional intermediaries where complexity exceeds ordinary citizens' direct experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinions should be based on objective reports not casual fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The author observes 'the number of public opinions based on any objective report was very small in proportion to those based on casual fancy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase reliance on objective reporting and verified information when forming public opinion; cultivate mechanisms that enlarge the share of opinions grounded in reliable reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against stereotyped images and legalistic deductive habits
rubrics_metrics.description: In self-contained communities 'public opinions . . . consisted chiefly of a few stereotyped images arranged in a pattern deduced from their legal and their moral codes,' producing static theorism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of letting fixed formulas, stereotypes, or legalistic deductions supplant factual inquiry; encourage updating premises from experience rather than spinning new rules from old abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that self-centered visions cause conflict when groups collide
rubrics_metrics.description: People 'see their own personal, class, dynastic, or municipal version of affairs' and when such self-centered groups 'rub against each other' the result is 'perpetual strife.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate conflict arising from mutually exclusive local or group-based worldviews; design forums and mediating institutions to surface, test, and reconcile competing perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional and technical reporting to expand the range of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes 'distant complexities are reported every day by engineers and accountants for business men, by secretaries and civil servants for officials, by intelligence officers for the General Staff, by some journalists for some readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on specialized reporting and institutional intermediaries (technical reports, civil service briefings, professional journalism) to translate distant, complex matters into materials usable for public judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct subjective vision through measurement and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Machiavelli saw that 'men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand' and lacked 'the materials for imagining a race of men that had learned how to correct their vision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt measurement, records, and analytical tools that can correct subjective impressions and biases—turn qualitative impressions into testable, comparable data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic ideals must be reconciled with the limits of political science
rubrics_metrics.description: Pioneering democrats 'did not possess the science for resolving the conflict between the known range of man's attention and their illimitable faith in his dignity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and institutional design should honestly confront the tension between democratic ideals of popular sovereignty and empirical limits on collective knowledge; build structures that augment, rather than assume, citizen capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the supply of civic information appropriate to the scale of governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 'the supply of information is to be left to casual experience' this only works if 'the environment must be confined within the range of every man's direct and certain knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match information provision to governance scale: local matters can rely more on casual, direct knowledge; national and international matters require systematic reporting, analysis, and institutional explanation.
